qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture fourteen. Tensors, and how to store the ones that are mostly empty.
Meet Sprout, a seed-swap app. Its thermometer shows eighteen degrees. One number is a scalar.
Sprout's thermometer: 18°. One number is a scalar.
One member rates four packets: three, five, one and four. That row is a vector.
One member's ratings, 3, 5, 1, 4: a vector.
Rows under rows make a matrix. Now you need a row and a column.
Rows under rows: a matrix. Two indices find a value.
A pile of grids is a tensor of order three. The order counts the indices you need.
A pile of grids is a 3-order tensor: three indices.
A seed packet has four features. A list like this is a vector.
A packet's features: one vector.
The soil sensor logs moisture and temperature over time: features by timestamps.
Sensor readings: features × timestamps, a matrix.
A photo is three grids, one per colour: width by height by channels.
A photo: width × height × channels (RGB).
A video is a row of photos, so frames by width by height by channels. That is order four.
A video: frames × width × height × channels.
Sprout's swap sheet has sixty-four cells, and only six are not zero. Its sparsity is ninety-one percent.
Sprout's swap sheet: 6 non-zeros of 64. Sparsity 91%.
Listing just the non-zeros, with row, column and value, takes eighteen numbers, not sixty-four.
Listing only the non-zeros: 18 numbers instead of 64.
Fill the sheet to fifty-two values. Now it is dense, with sparsity nineteen percent.
Fill it to 52: dense, sparsity 19%.
The list grows to one hundred and fifty-six numbers, more than the grid itself.
Now the list, 156 numbers, is bigger than the grid.
Real data is often sparse. Six members share only five of fifteen possible links.
A social graph: 5 links out of 15 possible.
Fault sensors report zero almost all of the time.
Fault sensors report 0 almost all the time.
With a million rows and columns, the grid has a million million cells. Far too big to store.
n ≈ a million: a million million cells. Too big to store.
So we keep only the non-zeros.
Keep only the non-zeros instead.
Store each non-zero with its position. Anything missing is zero.
Store only the non-zeros, each with its position.
A dictionary of keys maps each row and column pair to its value.
Dictionary of keys: each (row, column) key maps to its value.
Key three, one gives six. Key three, two is missing, so that cell is zero.
Look up key (3, 1): 6. A missing key means 0.
A coordinate list keeps the same facts as triples: row, column and value.
Coordinate list: a list of (row, column, value) tuples.
CSR reads the matrix row by row. V gets five, eight, three and six. Column index gets zero, one, two and one.
Read row by row: V = 5, 8, 3, 6; COL_INDEX = 0, 1, 2, 1.
Row index holds bookmarks: where each row starts in V. Zero, one, two, three and four.
ROW_INDEX marks where each row starts in V: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
Four rows need five bookmarks. The last one marks the end.
m rows need m + 1 bookmarks: the last marks the end.
Now read row two of this four by six matrix back.
Read row 2 of the slides' 4 × 6 matrix.
Its bookmarks say start at four and end at seven.
Start = ROW_INDEX[2] = 4, end = ROW_INDEX[3] = 7.
That slice holds fifty, sixty and seventy, in columns two, three and four.
Slice V: 50, 60, 70 at columns 2, 3, 4.
So row two is zero, zero, fifty, sixty, seventy, zero.
When two bookmarks are equal, the slice is empty and the row is all zeros.
Equal bookmarks, 2 and 2: an empty slice, an all-zero row.
CSC does the same, column by column. The values are ten, two, five, seven and nine.
CSC reads column by column: VALUES = 10, 2, 5, 7, 9.
Column pointer marks where each column starts: zero, two, three, four and five.
COL_PTR marks where each column starts: 0, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Column zero runs from zero to two: ten in row zero, and two in row three.
Column 0: from 0 to 2, so 10 at row 0 and 2 at row 3.
CSR makes rows fast. Ada's row lists her neighbours: Ben, Cy and Dot.
CSR: fast row operations. A graph row is one node's neighbours.
It suits row slicing and many matrix times vector products.
Good for row slicing and many A × x products.
CSC makes columns fast, like asking who swapped tomato.
CSC: fast column operations, like 'who swapped tomato?'
It suits huge datasets with many categorical features.
Good for huge datasets with many categorical features.
A tensor's order is how many indices find one value.
A sparse tensor is mostly zeros, so keep only the non-zeros.
CSR works by rows, and CSC by columns.
